The more she tried to recall what had happened, the more she found herself unable to escape the reminders, as if the shadows of that day were lurking in every corner, ready to pounce on her thoughts. vignette_attempts.vignette: Margaret, a 66-year-old shop owner from New Zealand, had always been proud of her successful business in a bustling part of town. However, a traumatic event had transformed her vibrant life into a struggle for normalcy. Two years prior, she had witnessed an incident of police violence that left her reeling. It had occurred one afternoon while she was closing her shop; she recalled the officers shouting and the sound of a man pleading for his life. That day, the sun had hung low in the sky, casting long shadows in the alley behind her store, and now every time the clock struck the same hour, Margaret felt a wave of anxiety wash over her. The memory of that day felt as vivid as the bruises she had seen on the man’s body, yet parts of the incident remained frustratingly elusive. The more she tried to recall what had happened, the more she found herself unable to escape the reminders, as if the shadows of that day were lurking in every corner, ready to pounce on her thoughts. The more vividly she recalled those details, the more frequently she found herself triggered; it was as if the memory had pulled her back into that moment, amplifying her anxiety. Each time she was triggered, Margaret felt an overwhelming urge to escape, leading her to compulsively shop in a misguided attempt to distract herself from the anxiety that surged within her. No matter how hard she concentrated, she could not recall the moments that led up to the violence; they felt like a jumbled puzzle locked away in her mind. In the wake of the incident, Margaret began to avoid circumstances that reminded her of that fateful day. She found herself steering clear of dark alleys and even the small park nearby where she used to relax. Each time she avoided these places, the memory of the incident crept closer, reinforcing her need to stay away, as if any reminder could trigger a flood of anxiety. These avoidance behaviors crystallized her belief that she was weak; every time she turned away from a trigger, the thought echoed in her mind that she could never be strong enough to face what had happened. Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgment of what had happened. The once familiar streets now felt like a maze of potential triggers. Walking past those dark alleys and the nearby park sent her mind racing back to that fateful day, the memories flooding in as if they were happening all over again. Additionally, she began to notice a compulsion to spend money impulsively, buying new merchandise for her shop with the hope that it would distract her from the haunting memories. Each purchase provided a fleeting comfort, but only deepened her sense of inadequacy when the thrill faded. Margaret believed that these reactions were a sign of weakness; she felt inadequate as a person and thought her inability to cope marked her as a bad coper. These negative self-assessments further fueled her anxiety, leading her to believe that perhaps she was going crazy. Every time her thoughts spiraled into self-criticism, it was like a flashback; she couldn't help but remember how helpless she felt during the incident, reinforcing her belief that she was weak. This conviction that she was fundamentally flawed made the memories sharper, as if she had to keep revisiting those moments to prove to herself the extent of her perceived failures. The thought that her mind was betraying her filled her with dread, and she felt isolated in her struggle. These reflections deepened her memory of the incident, reinforcing the narrative that she had not only failed to protect herself, but had also become someone who could not cope with the world around her. Each time she resorted to buying new merchandise in a bid to distract herself, she felt a quiet voice in her head reinforcing her belief that she needed to hide her weakness from the world. Each time Margaret felt dizzy or lightheaded—a sensation that had begun to plague her in the months following the event—she was reminded of the chaos of that day. It was as if her body was trying to replay the horror she could not fully remember, and the dizziness served as a reminder of her helplessness. The sensation would often strike her when she was alone in her shop, surrounded by the very products she had once loved selling. In those moments, her mind would flood with memories of the event, making her feel trapped and pushing her towards the impulsive buying that had become her way of coping. This cycle of memory and maladaptive strategy served to amplify her feelings of inadequacy; each purchase was a temporary escape, but when the thrill faded, she was left confronting the same haunting images that had driven her to buy in the first place. This created a vicious cycle; the triggers intensified her negative appraisals of herself, leading to further avoidance of situations that could potentially cause a panic attack. The more she leaned into her avoidance strategies, the more her memories felt like an inescapable prison, compounding her anxiety and pushing her further away from confronting what had happened. As the cycle continued, she noticed that the memories became more frequent, often triggered by ordinary moments that seemed innocuous but were steeped in her past. In turn, her memory gaps became more pronounced, and the fragments of the event felt increasingly unreal. The more she struggled to piece together what she had witnessed, the more inadequate she felt, stirring a deep-seated fear that she was losing her grip on reality. Despite her efforts to maintain a façade of normalcy, Margaret often found herself trapped in her own mind. This maladaptive strategy did little to alleviate her distress; instead, it compounded her feelings of inadequacy and fear.
